newsitem.title: CHILE: Quebrada Blanca copper output cut 50 pct by strike.
newsitem.headline: Quebrada Blanca copper output cut 50 pct by strike.

text.p: Production at Quebrada Blanca mine has been cut to about 50 percent of design capacity by a six-day-old strike but can maintain that level indefinitely if the walkout continues, general manager James Drake said.
Current inventories at the mine will last at least a few weeks at 75,000-tonne-a-year mine, Drake said.
"We've got staff doing leaching and electrowinning at about 50 percent of design capacity, or just over 100 tonnes a day of cathodes," he told Reuters.
"We expect to be able to maintain that rate and maybe improve it," he said.
Asked if the mine owned by Cominco Ltd will be able to meet its coming delivery commitments, Drake said, "For the moment, yes. We've got production inventory for at least a few weeks."
He said he did not want to comment on the possibility of a force majeure "unless we get to that point."
About 350 Quebrada Blanca workers, about 70 percent of the mine's workforce, walked off the job last Wednesday after their wage contract expired without renewal.
Marathon talks in Iquique over the weekend led nowhere, and Drake said the company had no plans to return to negotiations although its original wage offer still stood.

The union has been demanding a bonus over and above the "isolation bonus" which Quebrada Blanca currently pays to account for the site's extreme remoteness and altitude, said Drake. One of the highest mines in the world, it's located at about 4,200 meters above sea level on an uninhabited plateau near the Bolivian border.
"When they signed on, they accepted the isolation bonus as it was," he said. "They simply want something more than what we are prepared to offer."

He said the heart of the company's 37-month contract offer was a nine percent real salary increase now, plus three percent raises in each of the next two years, all on top of inflation which in Chile is running at about six percent a year.
"We feel we've got a fair offer on the table and we'll just wait. We're available if they want to come back and talk," he said.

He denied that a shortage of skilled labor in northern Chile was at the root of the strike. An explosion of new copper mines and expansions at existing pits has been widely attributed for a shortage of experienced miners in the Chilean copper industry and an upswing in strikes in the past year.
"Certainly the labor market is tight in Chile for skilled and experienced workers but I don't see that the strike is particularly motivated by that," he said.
